bluetooth_timeout.label: Turn Bluetooth off after (seconds)
bluetooth_timeout.description: When this controller is used over Bluetooth, turn Bluetooth off once no buttons have been pressed for this long. The next press turns it back on and reconnects. Use 0 to keep it on.

devices.vtechExpander: IO Expander from a VTech Guitar
devices.protarNeck: Rock Band Mustang Pro Guitar Neck

bluetooth_forget_hosts.description: Forgets the PCs, phones and consoles this controller has paired with over Bluetooth, so they have to pair again. Use this if a host removed the controller but still can't reconnect.
bluetooth_forget_hosts.title: Forget paired hosts?
bluetooth_forget_hosts.confirm_desc: This controller forgets every host it has paired with over Bluetooth and disconnects any that are connected now. Remove the controller from those hosts' Bluetooth settings too, then pair again. Controllers paired to this one are kept. This happens straight away, it can't be discarded.

midiOutput.controlNumber_desc: For example 4 for a hi-hat pedal, or 64 for a sustain pedal
midiOutput.fixedVelocity_desc: Always send this velocity, instead of one from how hard the input is hit

layout.resizeSidebar: Drag to resize sidebar (double-click to reset)

standbyLighting.description: The standby profile isn't a controller. Its LEDs light up while no other profile is active, like when the device isn't plugged into anything or is only charging, and it can pick the buttons that wake a sleeping console or PC. Only input, pattern, static and status LEDs work here, as there's no game or console to drive the rest.

whileSuspended.label: Also light up while the console or PC is asleep
whileSuspended.description: Normally the LEDs turn off when a console or PC goes to sleep with the controller still plugged in. With this on, the standby profile's LEDs take over instead. A sleeping console or PC only gives out a little power, so keep it to a few LEDs.

controllers.label: Connected controllers
controllers.description: Controllers plugged into this device (USB, Wii extension and so on) that the standby profile can read, so their buttons can light LEDs or wake a console or PC. Add the same ones the profile that uses them has. While that profile is active, the standby profile shares its controllers rather than taking them.

wake.label: Wake-up buttons
wake.description: Pressing one of these wakes up a console or PC that's asleep with the controller plugged in. Without any, the controller doesn't wake it at all. They can be on the connected controllers added above.

led_timeout.label: Turn LEDs off after (seconds)
led_timeout.description: Turn the LEDs off once no buttons have been pressed for this long, and back on with the next press. Use 0 to keep them on. Applies to the whole controller.

sleep_timeout.label: Sleep after (seconds)
sleep_timeout.description: Go to sleep once no buttons have been pressed for this long, while not plugged into USB. Press the wake button to wake back up. Use 0 to never sleep.

wake_active_high.label: Wake button is active high
wake_active_high.description: Turn this on if the wake button connects its pin to 3.3V rather than ground.

disconnectBluetoothOnSuspend.label: Disconnect Bluetooth controllers when the PC sleeps
disconnectBluetoothOnSuspend.description: When this profile's USB connection goes to sleep, disconnect the Bluetooth controllers using it so they turn off instead of running their batteries down. Turning a controller back on still wakes the PC.

invert_y_hid.label: Invert Y Axis for HID mode
invert_y_hid.description: Invert the Y Axis when in HID mode, as some apps expect it to be inverted.

syncCalibrations.label: Sync calibrations across inputs
syncCalibrations.description: Synchronise calibrations across inputs that are used multiple times. For example if you have whammy on multiple profiles, turning this on will keep your whammy calibration synchronised, while turning it off means you can have different calibrations per profile.

xinput_on_windows.label: Controller type on Windows (for USB)
xinput_on_windows.description: Pick if you wish to have your controllers emulate an XInput device or an HID device when plugged into a Windows PC. Note that this setting has no effect on macOS, Linux or on game consoles.
xinput_on_windows.clear_cache: If joy.cpl shows the controller blank after switching, run this registry fix and replug it.

ps4EmulationMode.label: Controller type on PS4/5
ps4EmulationMode.description: Pick the device type to emulate on PS4/5. PS3 works with Rock Band 4 without auth, but won't work in system menus or other games. PS4/5 works everywhere but requires authentication. For Fortnite Festival you can use a profile that emulates a keyboard to avoid needing auth.

legendMode.label: Icons to show
legendMode.description: Pick the icons to show below. This adjusts the icons and names shown in the UI, such as using A or B instead of Cross and Circle

combinedStrumDebounce.label: Combined strum debounce
combinedStrumDebounce.description: Strum up and down share one debounce window, so a strum is ignored while the other direction is still held or debouncing. Stops a bouncy strum switch registering a strum in the wrong direction. While this is on, changing one strum's debounce changes them all.

queueInputs.label: Queue fret and strum inputs
queueInputs.description: Inputs are read as fast as possible and every fret / strum change is queued, then sent one at a time so the game sees every change, even ones faster than its frame rate. Adds latency while the queue drains.

dequeueInterval.label: Dequeue interval (ms)
dequeueInterval.description: How long each queued state is held for. The game needs to run at {{fps}}+ fps to see every state.

xboxOneLegacyAdapter.label: Always emulate the Rock Band 4 Wireless Legacy Adapter on Xbox One/Series
xboxOneLegacyAdapter.description: Enabled by default for new configurations. On Xbox One/Series, emulates a Wireless Legacy Adapter so players can come and go without authenticating again, including swapping the authentication gamepad for a Guitar Hero Live guitar. Supports Rock Band 4 and Guitar Hero Live, with gamepad navigation outside games. When Xbox One mode is forced by a profile (eg for Fortnite Festival on Windows), it uses the native controller identity instead. Turn this off to use the native identity on consoles too.

selectToDpadLeft.label: Map Select to D-pad Left on Xbox One/Series, PS4/5 and Switch
selectToDpadLeft.description: Send Select as D-pad Left instead when plugged into an Xbox One/Series, PS4/5 or Switch.Rock Band 4 and Fortnite Festival can use D-pad Left to activate star power, which can work better than Select.

ps3OnRpcs3.label: Use USB passthrough with RPCS3
ps3OnRpcs3.description: Switch to PS3 mode when RPCS3 detects the controller, so it can be used with RPCS3's USB passthrough. Turn this off to keep the controller in its PC mode while RPCS3 is running.

fullRangeTurntableOnPc.label: Full range scratching on PC
fullRangeTurntableOnPc.description: Real Xbox 360 turntables only send a tiny range for scratching, which XInput's default deadzone hides on PC. When enabled, scratching uses the full range on PC, and stays accurate to a real turntable when plugged into an Xbox 360.

cymbalGlitchFix.label: Apply the cymbal glitch fix
cymbalGlitchFix.description: Rock Band 3 had a bug where hitting two cymbals at the same time would cause one of the cymbals to be dropped. This mitigates that bug, but may not work as well on Rock Band 2. This setting only applies on PS3 and Xbox 360.

device_to_emulate.label: Device to emulate
device_to_emulate.description: Pick the device to emulate. This is how you pick if you're emulating a guitar or gamepad.

device_name.label: Device name
device_name.description: What the whole controller is called over USB, shared by every profile. Over Bluetooth the profile's name is used, and this is only used when no profile is using Bluetooth. Leave it empty to use Santroller.

manufacturer_name.label: Manufacturer name
manufacturer_name.description: The USB manufacturer name, shared by every profile. Leave it empty to use sanjay900. KeyboardMania mode uses its required manufacturer name instead.

main.move_profile_up: Move up (profiles are checked in order)
main.move_profile_down: Move down (profiles are checked in order)

shifted.invertShift: Invert Shift (active when modifier is released)

cycle.description: Cycling inputs let you jump between a set list of values. This can be useful for something like the pickup selector, where you could map a button to the pickup selector, and each time you press the button, it jumps between each notch.
cycle.title: Cycling input {{id}}

custom.label: Custom notch thresholds
custom.description: Real 5-way pickup switches aren't evenly spaced. Move the switch to each notch and set the thresholds between them. When off, the range is split into 5 equal parts.

section.label: Axis range
section.description: Drive only part of the axis with this input, so two inputs (like a pair of triggers) can share it. Calibrate min as the input's resting position and max as fully pressed. Custom lets you pick the exact axis values to move between.

inputs.action_hold_hint: Actions default to a held input, so they need holding down for a moment and a stray press does nothing.

pollInterval.label: Poll interval (ms)
pollInterval.description: Time between platter reads (defaults to 5). The platter reports how far it moved since the last read, so this sets the velocity range: reading too often shrinks the readings. Minimum 1.

filters.title: Filters
filters.description: Run on every sample from the accelerometer, before any mapping uses it. For tilt, the gate and median remove strum bar hits, and a low pass around 5 - 10 Hz removes the vibration left over. Gyro readings are never filtered.

gate.label: Motion gate
gate.description: Ignores samples whose total acceleration is too far from gravity, as a strum bar hit or a bump causes them instead of tilt. The last good reading is held meanwhile.

median.label: Median
median.description: Uses the middle of the last few samples, so short spikes are dropped instead of being smoothed in.

lowPass.label: Low pass
lowPass.description: Smooths out vibration faster than the cutoff, more steeply than the low pass on a mapping. Lower cutoffs are smoother, but react more slowly.

turntablePollInterval.label: DJ Hero turntable poll interval (ms)
turntablePollInterval.description: Time between reads of a detected DJ Hero turntable (defaults to 5). The table velocities are movement since the last read, so reading too often shrinks them. Minimum 1.

debounce.label: Debounce
debounce.desc: Expressed in milliseconds (0.1ms steps), use 0 to disable

mode.label: Debounce applies to
mode.release_desc: presses register instantly, and the button stays held for the debounce time after letting go.
mode.press_desc: a press only counts once held for the debounce time, so ghost presses are ignored.
mode.impulse_desc: each press sends one tap lasting the debounce time, however long it's held.

holdTick.label: Hold Tick
holdTick.desc: Hold tick expresses how long an input is left active even if no input is detected

device_gate.description: Only enables this device while a pin reads a certain way, so devices on different connectors can share pins.
device_gate.active_low: Enabled while the pin is pulled low
device_gate.active_high: Enabled while the pin is pulled high

face_button_mapping_mode.label: Face Button Mapping Mode
face_button_mapping_mode.description: Face buttons are in different positions on different controllers. For example, if you were to use a Wii Classic controller on an Xbox 360, label based mode will map A to A and B to B, while position based mode would swap A with B and X with Y.

firmware.title: One firmware, configured live
firmware.body: Every board runs the same prebuilt firmware. The configurator sends your settings straight to the controller, so changes take effect immediately with no rebuilding or re-flashing.

devices.title: Devices
devices.body: Hardware attached to the board, such as a Wii Extension, USB Host, LEDs, Bluetooth or a multiplexer. Devices are shared by every profile. Buttons wired straight to pins don't need one.

profiles.title: Profiles
profiles.body: A profile holds the controller type to emulate, its input mappings, calibration and LEDs. You can have several, for example one for guitar and one for gamepad.

assignments.title: Assignments
assignments.body: Rules that decide when a profile is used: over USB, over Bluetooth, through an adapter, or when a button is held at startup.

steps.description: If your controller came from a seller with Santroller already installed, skip the first two steps.

flash.title: Put Santroller on your board
flash.body: Hold BOOTSEL while plugging the Pico in, download the UF2 for your chip (Pico 1 / RP2040 or Pico 2 / RP2350), and drag it onto the drive that appears (RPI-RP2 or RP2350). The board restarts by itself when the copy finishes.

wire.title: Wire up your hardware
wire.body: The Build Guides have pinouts and wiring steps for guitars, drums, turntables, adapters and LEDs. Check Supported Hardware if you're not sure which board or part to use.

connect.title: Connect to the configurator
connect.body: On the main page, click Connect to a Santroller powered device and pick your controller. On the website, use a Chromium-based browser such as Chrome or Edge, or download the desktop app.

update.title: Update the firmware if asked
update.body: If you see Controller firmware out of date, click Start Update. The update takes up to a minute. Don't unplug the controller until it reconnects.

devices.title: Add your devices
devices.body: On the Devices page, use the + button and choose Add device for each piece of hardware connected to the board, then set its pins. Skip this if everything is wired straight to pins.

profile.title: Set up a profile
profile.body: Select a profile under Profiles in the sidebar, or click Add profile. A new profile opens the Setup Profile wizard, which asks how the controller connects and what is plugged into it. Apply & Load Defaults fills in a sensible starting layout. Pick the controller type under Device to emulate in the profile's Settings.

inputs.title: Map your inputs
inputs.body: In the Inputs section, click Add Input, choose where the input comes from and set its Target Output. Detect Pin finds a pin for you when you press or move the control. For analog inputs such as whammy or tilt, open Axis Calibration and use Use current value to set the min, max and centre while watching the live value.

assignments.title: Check the assignments
assignments.body: The Assignments section controls when this profile is used. The wizard adds one for you; use Add Assignment for more, such as a Bluetooth or console-specific profile. A profile with no assignment is never used.

leds.title: Set up LEDs (optional)
leds.body: If you added an LED device, use Add LED / Display Mapping in the LEDs & Displays section to link LEDs to inputs and choose colours. Test All LEDs confirms the wiring and LED order.

standby.title: Standby profile (optional)
standby.body: A standby profile sets what the controller does when it isn't in use. Click Add standby profile under Profiles in the sidebar. Its LEDs light up while no other profile is active, like when the controller isn't plugged into anything or is only charging. Turn on Also light up while the console or PC is asleep to have them light up then too.

standbyWake.title: Wake a sleeping console or PC (optional)
standbyWake.body: The controller only wakes up a sleeping console or PC with the standby profile's Wake-up buttons. Without any, it won't wake it at all. If a button is on a controller plugged into this device (like a USB guitar), add that controller under Connected controllers first.

save.title: Save changes
save.body: Edits are sent to the controller as you make them so you can test straight away, but they are only stored once you click Save changes at the top of the page.

backup.title: Back up your config
backup.body: On the main page, Export Current Config downloads your settings as a file. Load Config from File restores it later, including onto another board. Bluetooth pairings aren't included.

saveReminder.title: Remember to save
saveReminder.body: The Save changes button only appears when there is something to save. If you unplug the controller before saving, it goes back to its last saved config.

simpleMode.title: Simple mode and Advanced mode
simpleMode.body: Controllers set up by a seller may open in Simple mode, which hides the Devices, Pin Labels and Debug pages so you can't break the wiring setup by accident. Click Switch to Advanced Mode on the main page to see everything.

desktopApp.title: Website or desktop app
desktopApp.body: Both do the same job. The website needs a browser with WebHID (Chrome, Edge or another Chromium browser). The desktop app works anywhere and can install the Linux udev rules for you.

sharedPins.title: Swappable connectors on the same pins
sharedPins.body: Devices that are never plugged in at the same time, like a PS2 port and a SNES port on a modular adapter, can share pins. Turn on Enable with a pin on each device, and have each connector set that pin differently: tied high or low, or to its own voltage on an analog pin. Only the device that's plugged in is used, and swapping connectors switches over by itself.

peripherals.title: Running out of pins
peripherals.body: A second Pico can act as a Peripheral, connected over I2C, to add more inputs and devices. Add it from the Devices page; it then gets its own page in the sidebar.

labels.title: Naming your pins
labels.body: The Pin Labels page lets you name pins, LEDs and multiplexer or matrix channels, so mappings read as "Green fret" instead of a pin number.

items.notFound: Controller doesn't show up: a blank board must have the UF2 flashed first (step 1). On the website, make sure you're using a Chromium-based browser.
items.linux: Linux: install the udev rules from the main page, then unplug and replug the controller.
items.notResponding: Controller not responding: open the Debug page, click Copy logs, and share them on the Discord.
items.profileInactive: Inputs do nothing: check that the profile has an assignment and shows the Active badge in the sidebar.
items.lostChanges: Settings reset after unplugging: click Save changes before unplugging.
items.newerFirmware: Firmware is newer than the configurator: refresh the website, or update the desktop app.

santroller1.title: Coming from Santroller 1?
santroller1.body: If your Pico is already running Santroller 1, you don't need to hold BOOTSEL. Connect to it in Santroller 1 and click "Revert Device to Arduino", which puts the Pico into bootloader mode so the RPI-RP2 or RP2350 drive shows up. If you want to bring your config with you, make sure you export your presets from Santroller 1. You can then import the .picoconfig files into Santroller 2.

assignmentsGuide.subtitle: Santroller 2 can hold many profiles. Assignments are the rules that decide which profiles are active, what each one talks to, and which connected controllers it reads from.

rules.title: A profile is only used when one of its rules matches
rules.body: Each profile has one or more rules. A profile with no rules is never used, and a profile whose rules don't match right now sits idle until they do.

and.title: Everything in a rule must be true
and.body: A rule is a list of conditions, such as USB and a Wii guitar is plugged into the adapter. The rule only matches when all of them are true at once.

or.title: Any one rule is enough
or.body: Extra rules are alternatives, shown with OR between them. The first rule that matches is used and the rest are ignored.

claim.title: A matching profile claims what it uses
claim.body: When a rule matches, its profile claims the connected controllers in that rule and any Bluetooth or console port it outputs to. Nothing else can use a claimed device, so profiles higher in the sidebar get first pick. USB output is the exception: any number of profiles can share it.

pins.title: Board pins don't need assigning
pins.body: Buttons, sensors and peripherals wired directly to the board are available to every profile unless a profile claims them with Claim directly wired inputs. Only external controllers and adapters need to be added to a rule.

anatomy.title: What goes in a rule
anatomy.description: Every rule on the Profiles page is a card with the same three steps. A rule needs at least one condition, and the target connection is the one almost every rule has.

target.body: How this device presents itself to the console or PC: USB, Bluetooth, the PS1/2 port, a Wii extension, the GameCube / N64 port or the SNES / NES port. Bluetooth needs a board with Bluetooth, and the console port targets only match once a console is actually talking to the device on that port.

source.body: An external controller this profile reads from: a Wii extension, a PS1/2 controller, a USB or Bluetooth controller (by type or a specific device), or a MIDI channel. The rule only matches while a matching controller is connected and no other profile has claimed it, and each one gets a slot number that your inputs use to read from it.

trigger.body: An optional button condition, either held at startup or pressed any time. Use it to switch between profiles from the controller itself.

anatomy.exampleTitle: Example: a profile with two rules
anatomy.exampleCaption: This profile is used over USB when a Wii guitar is plugged in, or over Bluetooth with no Wii guitar needed. Here a Wii guitar is plugged in over USB, so Rule #1 shows as matching. If both could match, Rule #1 wins because it comes first. The bar at the top of each card sums up the whole rule.

multiSource.title: Several controllers in one rule
multiSource.description: A rule can list more than one connected controller. The profile then reads from all of them at once, and you can map each input from whichever controller suits it best.
multiSource.exampleTitle: Example: MIDI drum kit with a gamepad for navigation
multiSource.exampleIntro: An electronic drum kit is great for playing but has no way to press Start or move through menus. Put the kit and a USB gamepad in the same rule, and the console sees one drum controller that gets its pads from the kit and its buttons from the gamepad.
multiSource.mappingTitle: Then map your inputs from the matching slot
multiSource.mappingMidi: Drum pads and cymbals come from {{slot}}, using the kit's note numbers.
multiSource.mappingGamepad: Start, Select, Home and the D-pad come from {{slot}}.

notes.allRequired: Every controller in a rule has to be connected and unclaimed for it to match, which is why Rule #2 is there. Slot numbers are shared between rules, so your pad mappings keep working whichever rule matched.
notes.midiSeen: A MIDI channel only counts as connected once the kit has sent something on it. After plugging in, hit a pad and the profile will pick it up.
notes.hub: Two USB devices on the host port need a USB hub. If your kit has a 5-pin MIDI output, you can use a MIDI DIN input instead and leave the USB port free for the gamepad.
notes.anyCombo: The same idea works with any mix of sources, such as a Wii guitar with a USB gamepad for navigation.

multiSource.exampleCaption: Rule #2 is optional. It lets the kit work on its own when the gamepad isn't plugged in.

selection.title: How profiles get chosen
selection.description: Assignments are re-checked whenever the device starts, a controller is plugged in or unplugged, the console mode changes, or an any-time trigger is pressed.

order.title: Profiles are checked from top to bottom
order.body: Each profile tries its rules in order and uses the first one that matches. Profile order is the order they appear in the sidebar.

exclusive.title: Bluetooth, PS1/2, Wii, GameCube / N64 and SNES / NES targets go to one profile
exclusive.body: Those ports can only act as one controller, so the first matching profile claims the port. Later profiles that ask for the same target won't match while it's claimed.

usb.title: USB can be shared
usb.body: Every profile whose rule matches over USB becomes active at the same time, and the console or PC sees one controller per profile on the same cable. This is how a single board can act as several players, but it also means two profiles with plain USB rules will both show up.

claim.title: Each connected controller is claimed by one profile
claim.body: When a rule matches, its profile claims the controllers it used, and a claimed controller can't be read by any other profile. If more identical controllers are still unclaimed, the same profile is used again for each of them, so two USB guitars through a hub give you two players from one profile.

localInputs.title: Directly wired inputs can be claimed too
localInputs.body: Turn on Claim directly wired inputs in a rule and it claims the buttons and sensors wired to this board, so it only matches if no profile above it has already claimed them. Use it when several profiles output the same inputs over different connections but only one should be active at a time. USB rules only match while a PC or console is connected, so a USB profile placed above a Bluetooth one takes over when plugged in and hands back to Bluetooth when running from a battery or charger.

auto.behaviour: Matches on any console or PC, and the device works out which console it is plugged into. This is the right choice for most profiles.

forced.behaviour: Skips console detection and always uses the chosen mode while this profile is active. If the configurator is open, the switch waits until you close it.

specific.behaviour: Only matches once the device has detected that console. Use it for a profile that should only apply on, say, a PS3.

boot.behaviour: Only matches if the button is held as the device starts up or changes console mode. The choice lasts until the next restart.

anytime.behaviour: Pressing the button re-checks the assignments straight away with this rule matching, so you can switch profiles mid-session. The profile stays active until the next re-check.

inverted.behaviour: Flips the button condition, so the rule matches when the button is not held. Pair it with a normal trigger to make an either-or switch.

slots.title: Slots
slots.body: Every connected controller or adapter you add to a profile gets a slot number, such as Slot 1: USB Host (Guitar). When you map an input from an external controller, you pick the slot it comes from. Slot numbers are counted per kind of controller across the whole profile, so the same slot means the same controller whichever rule matched.
slots.migrate: Profiles made with older versions numbered slots separately in each rule. The Profiles page shows a Migrate slot numbering button for these, and it moves your inputs across for you.

usb.title: A plain USB controller
usb.body: One profile with one rule: USB (Auto-detect). Everything wired to the board's pins just works.

adapter.title: A Wii or PS1/2 adapter
adapter.body: One rule with USB and the controller type as a connected controller, for example Wii Extension: Guitar. The adapter only works with the controller types your profiles list, so add another profile with Wii Extension: Drums if you want it to support drums, and one for each other controller type you want to use.

wiredWireless.title: Different settings over USB and Bluetooth
wiredWireless.body: Make two profiles: one with a USB rule and one with a Bluetooth rule, and turn on Claim directly wired inputs in both. Put the USB profile first. While plugged into a PC or console the USB profile claims the inputs and Bluetooth stays off, and on a battery or charger the Bluetooth profile takes over. Without the toggle, both are active while plugged in and you'd get two controllers.

festivalWired.title: Holding a button at startup to change profiles (direct wired)
festivalWired.body: For a guitar with everything wired to the board's pins, make a keyboard profile such as a Fortnite Festival layout and a normal guitar profile, and turn on Claim directly wired inputs in both. Put the keyboard profile first and give it Hold Button at Startup. Holding the button while plugging in makes the keyboard profile claim the inputs, so the guitar profile can't match and the PC only sees a keyboard. Plug in without holding it and the guitar profile claims them instead. The choice lasts until the guitar is unplugged.

festivalAdapter.title: Holding a button at startup to change profiles (adapter)
festivalAdapter.body: When the guitar comes through an adapter, such as a Wii guitar on a Wii adapter, add it as a connected controller to both profiles instead, for example Wii Extension: Guitar. Put the keyboard profile first with Hold Button at Startup, using a button on the guitar. Once the keyboard profile has claimed the adapter's controller, the guitar profile can't match. Claim directly wired inputs isn't needed here, since the inputs come from the adapter rather than the board's pins.

twoPlayers.title: Two USB guitars through one board
twoPlayers.body: One profile with USB and USB Host (By Type): Guitar. Each guitar plugged in is claimed by its own copy of the profile, and the console sees two guitars.

items.noRule: A profile with no rules, or no target connection, is never used. The Profiles page warns about both.
items.notConnected: A rule with a connected controller only matches while that controller is plugged in, detected, and not claimed by a profile higher up the list. Check the Devices page to see what the board can see.
items.taken: If a profile never activates over Bluetooth or a console port, a profile higher up the list probably claimed that port first.
items.duplicate: If the PC sees more controllers than you expect, more than one profile matched over USB. Add a trigger or a connected-controller condition so only the one you want matches.
items.slotMissing: If a controller doesn't appear when mapping an input, add it under Connected Controller / Adapter in that profile's rules first.
items.localInputs: If a profile with Claim directly wired inputs turned on never activates, a profile higher up the list with the same toggle probably claimed the inputs first. Reorder them so the one you'd rather use comes first.

firmwareDifferences.title: Firmware Differences (Santroller 2 vs Santroller 1)
firmwareDifferences.subtitle: A comprehensive breakdown of architectural changes, hardware support, and new features between Santroller 2 and the legacy Ardwiino/Santroller 1 firmware.

multiProfile.santroller1: One configuration per controller, with button-combo switching between console emulation modes. Changing bindings or controller type meant rebuilding and re-flashing the firmware.
multiProfile.santroller2: Multiple profiles with conditional Assignments (USB, Bluetooth, console mode, connected extensions), switchable at runtime without re-flashing.

configBuilds.santroller1: The configurator saved configs as .picoconfig files, then generated a config header and compiled a custom firmware build (PlatformIO) for every configuration change. This required around a gigabyte of compilers and toolchains to be downloaded onto your machine.
configBuilds.santroller2: A single prebuilt firmware. Configuration is sent to the device at runtime as Protocol Buffers (nanopb on device, protobuf.js in the configurator), so changes apply instantly without a rebuild, and no compilers or toolchains need to be installed.

rp2040.santroller1: Primary platform, built on the Arduino-Pico core with multicore, PIO USB and PIO-driven LEDs.
rp2040.santroller2: Rewritten directly on the Pico SDK 2.x in C++ with a modular device, emulation and profile framework.

rp2350.santroller1: Supported (Pico 2 and Pico 2 W builds, including secondary-Pico builds).
rp2350.santroller2: Supported (Pico 2 and Pico 2 W), using the same prebuilt firmware approach as RP2040.

avr.feature: Legacy AVR Microcontrollers (Pro Micro / Leonardo / Uno / Mega)
avr.santroller1: Supported (ATmega32U4 directly; Uno/Mega via the ATmega16U2 USB chip).
avr.santroller2: Not supported. RP2040/RP2350 is required. AVR boards stay on the legacy firmware (v10.1.189-legacy).

firmwareUpdates.santroller1: The desktop configurator compiled and flashed firmware over USB.
firmwareUpdates.santroller2: In-browser updates over USB, plus Bluetooth FOTA (Firmware Over-The-Air) on Pico W / Pico 2 W.

usbHost.santroller1: PIO USB host with hub support, Xbox 360 wired and wireless receivers, PS4/PS5 controllers, generic HID devices and USB MIDI.
usbHost.santroller2: Reworked TinyUSB + Pico-PIO-USB host stack, adding Xbox One wireless adapters, OG Xbox controllers and USB Bluetooth dongles.

consoleEmulation.santroller1: XInput, Xbox One, OG Xbox, PS2 (via PS3 adapters and on AVR), PS3, PS4/PS5, Switch, Wii (RB and extension emulation), PC HID, Raphnet and Fortnite Festival modes.
consoleEmulation.santroller2: Modular emulators for all of the above, plus Joybus (N64/GC), SNES and Wii Remote over Bluetooth.

consoleAuth.santroller1: PS4 and Xbox One authentication passthrough using a connected USB controller, and PS5 authentication via a P5General.
consoleAuth.santroller2: The same USB passthrough authentication (including PS5 via a P5General), plus support for dedicated Xbox One security chips over I2C.

festival.santroller1: Festival was a separate emulation type with a single hardcoded mapping that could not be customised.
festival.santroller2: Festival is a profile like any other, so it can have its own layout and bindings and be selected by Assignments alongside your standard profiles.

bluetooth.santroller1: Pico W BLE HID gamepad and keyboard/mouse emulation, plus Bluetooth input from another Santroller.
bluetooth.santroller2: BTstack integration on Pico W and USB Bluetooth dongles, adding Wii Remote emulation alongside the BLE gamepad and keyboard profiles.

inputPipeline.santroller1: Debouncing, deadzones, multipliers, analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog conversion, joystick-to-dpad and macros.
inputPipeline.santroller2: Reworked input manager with the same processing options, plus custom analog range remapping.

coreDevices.feature: Core Instruments, Peripherals & LEDs (Already Supported in v1)
coreDevices.santroller1: Already supported: MPR121 fret sensing, analog multiplexers, matrix keypads, rotary encoders, APA102 & WS2812 RGB LEDs, STP16CPC constant-current LED drivers, I2C accelerometers, GH5 tap bars, DJ Hero turntables, WT/BH drums, CRKD guitar necks, and MAX1704x battery monitors.
coreDevices.santroller2: All ported to the modular device framework with unified pin assignments, per-device configuration, and profile-aware mapping.

newDevices.santroller2: Switch Network (paired pin key matrix), Xbox 360 RF front panel module, Joybus controller input (N64 / GameCube), SNES/NES controller input, ADS1115 ADCs, Infinium optical crossfaders, DMX512 lighting output, CRKD drum kits, and VTech guitar expanders.

configurator.santroller1: Desktop Avalonia (C#) application for Windows, macOS and Linux.
configurator.santroller2: Web app using WebHID and Web Bluetooth, with no install required. On phones, Bluetooth-capable controllers can be configured over Web Bluetooth (Chrome on Android, Bluefy on iOS).

buildGuides.santroller1: A static written guide on santroller.com. You followed the steps, then configured everything separately in the configurator.
buildGuides.santroller2: Interactive guides built into the configurator that set up your configuration as you go, testing each input as you wire it.

multiProfile.title: Multi-Profile & Assignments
multiProfile.body: In Santroller 1, each controller had one configuration (with button-combo console mode switching), and changing it meant rebuilding and re-flashing the firmware. Santroller 2 introduces Profiles paired with conditional Assignments, so a single controller can use different bindings depending on the console mode, connection type, or which guitar neck or USB device is plugged in.

protobuf.title: Protocol Buffers & Nanopb
protobuf.body: Santroller 1 compiled your configuration directly into a custom firmware build every time you changed it, which meant downloading around a gigabyte of compilers and toolchains first. Santroller 2 ships one prebuilt firmware and sends configuration, commands, and debug data at runtime as Google Protocol Buffers (nanopb), so changes apply instantly and the schema can grow without breaking existing configs.

usbHost.title: Modern USB Host & PIO USB
usbHost.body: Santroller 2 reworks the TinyUSB + PIO USB host stack. Alongside the hubs, Xbox 360 wireless receivers, PlayStation controllers, and USB MIDI devices supported in Santroller 1, it adds Xbox One wireless adapters, OG Xbox controllers, and USB Bluetooth dongles.

picoSdk.title: Native Pico SDK Rewrite
picoSdk.body: Santroller 1 was built on the Arduino-Pico core. Santroller 2 is rewritten directly on the Raspberry Pi Pico SDK 2.x, with a modular framework for devices, console emulators, and profiles on both RP2040 and RP2350.

fota.title: FOTA (Firmware Over-The-Air)
fota.body: On wireless hardware (Pico W and Pico 2 W), Santroller 2 includes a FOTA bootloader, so firmware can be updated over Bluetooth from the web configurator without plugging the controller in.

webConfigurator.title: Web & Mobile Configurator
webConfigurator.body: Replaced the desktop Avalonia (C#) application with a zero-install web app using WebHID (for USB) and Web Bluetooth. You can configure controllers, map inputs, test sensors, and update firmware from a desktop browser, and Bluetooth-capable controllers can also be configured from mobile phones (Chrome on Android, Bluefy on iOS). The build guides are interactive too, configuring your controller step by step as you wire it.

avrDeprecation.title: Microcontroller Hardware Deprecation
avrDeprecation.body: Santroller 1 originated as "Ardwiino" and still supports 8-bit AVR microcontrollers like the ATmega32U4 (Arduino Leonardo / SparkFun Pro Micro) and ATmega16U2 (Arduino Uno / Mega). Due to their limited flash and RAM (32 KB / 2.5 KB on the ATmega32U4), AVR chips cannot support multi-profile storage, protocol buffers, USB host stacks, or Bluetooth emulation. Santroller 2 requires a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040) or Pico 2 (RP2350). Existing AVR builds should remain on the legacy Santroller 1 firmware (v10.1.189-legacy.3).

matrix.title: Technical Specifications Comparison
matrix.description: Side-by-side comparison of capabilities between legacy Ardwiino / Santroller 1 and the new Santroller 2 firmware.

migration.title: Migrating from Santroller 1 to Santroller 2
migration.description: If you have existing controllers configured with Santroller 1, here is what you need to know about migrating your configuration and hardware.

configImport.title: Automated Legacy Config (.picoconfig) Import
configImport.body: The Santroller Configurator provides an automated import tool for legacy .picoconfig files. It translates legacy bindings, pins, axis thresholds, multipliers, and peripheral definitions into Santroller 2 Profiles and Assignments.

pinout.title: Pinout Compatibility
pinout.body: If you already built a controller using a Raspberry Pi Pico on Santroller 1, your physical wiring stays the same. Flash Santroller 2 and import your .picoconfig (or set up your existing GPIO pins manually) without re-soldering.

avr.title: Legacy AVR Boards (Pro Micro / Uno)
avr.body: If your controller is built on an ATmega32U4 (Pro Micro) or ATmega16U2 (Uno/Mega), it cannot run Santroller 2. You can continue using the legacy Santroller 1 configurator and firmware at <legacyLink>legacy.santroller.com</legacyLink>. For new builds or upgrades, drop-in replacement RP2040 boards (such as RP2040-Zero or Pro Micro RP2040 pin-compatible clones) are strongly recommended.

mpr121.digital_description: Only electrodes 4 to 11 support GPIO. Touch sensing must stop before the first electrode used as GPIO.

display.controller_description: The chip on the display. Most 0.96" displays are SSD1306, most 1.3" displays are SH1106, 2.42" displays are usually SSD1309, and 128 x 128 or 128 x 64 portrait displays (eg the Adafruit 128 x 64 FeatherWing) are usually SH1107. If the picture is shifted by a couple of pixels with a column of noise at the edge, try SH1106 or SSD1306 instead.
display.address_description: Most displays are 0x3C. Some have a jumper or resistor on the back to change it to 0x3D, so two can share a bus.
display.rotation_description: Turns everything on the display clockwise, for displays mounted upside down or sideways. Positions on the display are after turning it. 64 x 128 panels are usually turned 90 degrees.
display.shown_description: Shown while this LED would be on, eg while its button is held, once authentication is done, or whenever this profile is active for an always on LED. Later LEDs are drawn over earlier ones.
display.bar_description: Filled by how bright this LED would be, eg how far an axis is pushed or how full star power is. Later LEDs are drawn over earlier ones.
display.text_description: Up to {{count}} characters, letters, numbers and symbols only. Each one is 6 x 8 pixels at size 1.
display.image_description: Scaled down to fit the display. Bright pixels light up, turn on Invert for dark images on a light background.
display.preview_description: Every LED on this display in this profile, as if they were all on. The outline is this one, drag it to move it, or use the arrow keys (hold Shift for 8 pixels at a time).
display.preview_move: Display preview, drag or use the arrow keys to move this LED

joybus.description: Wire a 1k resistor between the data pin and 3.3V. Without it the line is only held up by the weak internal pull-up, which can cause the stick to jump around.

battery.description: Estimates the battery level from its voltage, and reports it over Bluetooth. For a battery level that accounts for how the voltage drops under load, use a MAX1704X fuel gauge instead.
battery.pin_description: GP29 reads VSYS on a Pico through its built-in divider. On a Pico W, GP29 can only be read while Bluetooth is set up, as it is shared with the wireless chip.
battery.divider_description: How much the battery voltage is divided down before the pin. GP29's VSYS divider is 3.
battery.full_description: The level goes in a straight line between these. 3300 to 4200 mV suits a single LiPo cell.

powerManagement.description: Controls a battery module (eg a TP4056 charger with a boost converter) based on how long it has been since the last button press.

heartbeat.title: Keep alive
heartbeat.description: Pulses a pin while the controller is in use, drawing a little extra current every so often so power banks that turn off under a light load stay on.

inactivity.title: Turn off
inactivity.description: Drives a pin once the controller hasn't been used for a while, to turn the module off. Either hold it on (e.g. for a MOSFET), or pulse it to press the module's power button.
inactivity.not_on_usb: Only when not plugged into USB
inactivity.pulse_count_description: How many times to press the power button: 1 for a single press, 2 for a double press, and so on. Use 0 to hold the pin on instead

xbox360Rf.description: Sets up an Xbox 360 RF module (the console's wireless receiver board) and lets you sync controllers to it. Wire its USB lines to a USB Host device to receive the controller inputs.

type.label: Module Type
type.description: The original (fat) console module, or the 360 Slim module

hostPower.label: USB Host 5V Power
hostPower.description: For Adafruit Feather boards with USB Host. Turns on the Feather's built-in 5V boost converter, which powers the USB host port.

selector.label: Pin order
selector.description: D+ and D- need to be next to each other, but you can choose if D+ is first or D- is first.

address.label: Address
address.description: Must match the secondary Pico: 0x75 if its ID pin is left unconnected, or 0x76 if its ID pin is connected to GND. Use different addresses to read two secondary Picos at once.

leds.invert_desc: Invert output pin logic so active-low LEDs work (low = on, high = off)

overlay.label: Overlay
overlay.description: Only takes over the LED while active. The rest of the time, earlier mappings on the same LED or the game show through.

hides.title: Hides another LED mapping
hides.off_colour: This mapping shares an LED with {{leds}}. It shows its released colour whenever it isn't active, so {{leds}} never shows. Turn on "Overlay" here so the earlier mappings show through while this input is released.
hides.always: This mapping shares an LED with {{leds}}. It updates that LED all the time, so {{leds}} never shows. When mappings share an LED, only the last one in the list is visible.

pwmShared.title: Shares a PWM output
pwmShared.body: This pin shares its PWM output with {{leds}}, as pins 16 apart (like GP0 and GP16) do, so they always show the same brightness. Move one of them to another pin.

cutsShort.title: Takes over an LED the game controls
cutsShort.off_colour: This mapping shares an LED with {{leds}}, which the game controls. It shows its released colour whenever it isn't active, taking the LED back about a second after the game last changed it, so the game's colour barely shows. Turn on "Overlay" here so this mapping only takes the LED while the input is pressed.
cutsShort.always: This mapping shares an LED with {{leds}}, which the game controls. It updates that LED all the time, so the game's colour only shows for about a second each time the game changes it.

leds.mpr121_pin_description: Electrodes 4 to 11 can drive an LED. Touch sensing stops before the first electrode used this way, so wire touch inputs to the lower electrodes.

assignments.localInputsDesc: Claims the buttons and sensors wired straight to this board's pins. Controllers in this profile's rules, like a PS1/2 controller or Wii extension, are claimed already, so this is only needed for inputs that aren't on one. Only one profile can claim them at a time, and the highest one in the sidebar wins.

assignments.xboxOneAuthDesc: Plug in an Xbox One controller to authenticate this rule with an Xbox, then swap it for the instrument. assignments.missingDevice: This profile is missing an emulation assignment. Without one, Santroller doesn't know when it should use this profile, so it won't be used.
assignments.missing: This profile is missing an assignment! Without one, it won't ever be assigned.
assignments.oldSlotIds: This profile numbers its slots separately in each assignment list, so the same slot number can mean a different device depending on which list matched. Migrating gives every slot its own number across the profile and moves your inputs to match. Inputs that read a slot that was a different device in each list are copied so each one keeps working.

wireless.title: Wireless: Bluetooth & Battery (Pico W)
wireless.subtitle: LiPo Battery Power and Bluetooth Output on a Pico W / Pico 2 W
wireless.description: Run your controller from a single-cell LiPo battery and pair it with a PC or phone over Bluetooth, with battery level reporting and sleep when idle. USB keeps working too.

board.title: Which Pico is this?
board.desc: Santroller runs the same firmware on wireless and non-wireless Picos, so the configurator can't tell whether the wireless chip is fitted. Pick your board:
board.chipUnknown: Connect your Pico to see which chip it uses.
board.identify: A genuine Pico W / Pico 2 W has a silver metal shield with the Raspberry Pi logo over its wireless chip.
board.unknownPrompt: Pick your board to enable the Bluetooth setup.
board.plainWarning: A Pico without the wireless chip can't be a Bluetooth controller on its own, so the Bluetooth setup is disabled. Santroller can use a supported USB Bluetooth adapter on a USB host port instead, which this guide doesn't cover. The battery and sleep steps still apply.

wireless-intro.title: Supplies, Overview & Safety
wireless-intro.description: What a wireless build gives you, what it needs, and how to handle LiPo batteries safely.
wireless-intro.intro: A Pico W or Pico 2 W has a CYW43439 wireless chip that Santroller uses to act as a Bluetooth (BLE) gamepad. Add a LiPo battery and the controller can go fully wireless, while USB keeps working whenever it is plugged in.
getList: Bluetooth controller: The Pico advertises as a BLE gamepad called SantrollerBT, which PCs and phones can pair with directly.
USB and Bluetooth at once: The same profile keeps working over USB, so you can still play wired, update firmware and configure over the cable.
Battery level: The battery percentage is reported to the paired host through the standard Bluetooth battery service.
Power saving: Bluetooth can turn off, and the Pico can sleep, when the controller is left unused.
wireless-intro.consoleNote: Most consoles won't pair with a Bluetooth gamepad. To play on one, a second Pico W plugged into the console can act as the receiver (give its profile a Bluetooth controller slot on the Inputs page). For a Wii, the Inputs page also has a Wii Remote Bluetooth mode.
requiresList: A genuine Pico W or Pico 2 W: Bluetooth needs the CYW43439 wireless chip. Plain Picos, and clone "Pico W" boards with an ESP8266 / ESP8285 chip, have no Bluetooth radio Santroller can use.
USB access: Keep the Pico's USB port reachable in the finished controller for configuring, firmware updates and charging.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico W or Pico 2 W
Single-cell 3.7V LiPo / Li-ion battery with a built-in protection circuit
Single-cell LiPo charger board with protection (eg a TP4056 module with protection)
Schottky diode rated for at least 1A and over 10V reverse voltage (eg 1N5817 or 1N5819)
Optional: MAX17043 / MAX17048 fuel gauge board for a more accurate battery percentage
Optional: power switch for the battery output
Soldering Iron, Wire & Multimeter
safetyList: Use a protected cell and a proper charger: Only charge a LiPo with a charger made for single-cell lithium batteries, and use a cell or charger board with over-discharge, over-current and short circuit protection.
Never connect the battery to 3V3 or VBUS: The battery only goes to VSYS (pin 39), through a Schottky diode. 3V3 (pin 36) is the Pico's regulator output and VBUS (pin 40) is the USB 5V line.
Check the polarity: Reversing the battery leads can destroy the charger and the Pico. Battery connector colours aren't always standard, so check + and − with a multimeter before connecting.
Don't short or puncture the cell: Insulate every joint, keep the battery away from sharp edges and screws, and secure it so it can't move inside the controller.
Retire damaged cells: Disconnect a swollen, dented or hot battery straight away and take it to a battery recycling point. Don't leave a LiPo charging unattended near anything flammable.

wireless-battery.title: Battery Wiring & Level Sensing
wireless-battery.description: Wire the charger and battery to VSYS through a Schottky diode, then pick how the battery level is measured.
wiringSteps: Battery to charger: With nothing plugged in, solder the LiPo to the charger board's battery pads (B+ / B−, sometimes BAT+ / BAT−).
Charger to diode: Wire the charger board's protected output (OUT+) to the diode's anode (the end without the stripe). If you're adding a power switch, put it in this wire.

Diode to VSYS: Wire the diode's cathode (the striped end) to VSYS (pin 39). The diode stops USB's 5V from flowing back into the battery, and the Pico's own diode stops the battery feeding back into USB.
Ground: Wire the charger's OUT− to any Pico GND, eg pin 38.

Charging: Charge through the charger board's own USB socket. To charge from the Pico's USB port instead, feed the charger's IN+ from VBUS (pin 40) and IN− from GND, but only if its charge current is within what your USB port can supply (many TP4056 boards default to 1A, set by their RPROG resistor).
Check before powering up: With USB unplugged, measure VSYS to GND with a multimeter. It should read the battery voltage minus the diode's drop (a few tenths of a volt).
pinRows: Diode cathode (striped end), fed from the charger's OUT+
Optional: charger IN+, only to charge from the Pico's USB port
wireless-battery.sensorDesc: Pick how the Pico measures the battery. The level is reported to the paired host over Bluetooth.
wireless-battery.adcInfo: GP29 reads VSYS through the Pico's built-in divide-by-3, so it needs no extra wiring. It reads after the diode, so it sees the battery voltage minus the diode's drop, and while USB is plugged in it reads the USB voltage instead and shows full. The level is a straight line between the empty and full voltages (3300 to 4200 mV suits one LiPo cell); lower both by your diode's drop for a closer reading.
wireless-battery.adcPicoW: On a Pico W, GP29 is shared with the wireless chip, so it can only be read while Bluetooth is set up (the next step).
wireless-battery.gaugeInfo: A MAX17043 / MAX17048 style fuel gauge measures the cell itself and works out a more accurate percentage. Connect its battery side as your board's markings show, and wire it to the Pico on its own I2C bus:
gaugeWiring: Pull-ups: SDA and SCL must be pulled up to 3.3V, never to the battery. If your board's pull-ups go to the battery voltage, remove them and fit 4.7kΩ pull-ups to 3V3 (pin 36) instead.
wireless-battery.addGaugeBtn: Add MAX1704x Fuel Gauge on GP{{sda}} / GP{{scl}}
wireless-battery.otherSensorAdc: A GP29 battery monitor is already set up. Remove it on the Devices page first, so only one sensor reports the battery level.
wireless-battery.otherSensorGauge: A MAX1704x fuel gauge is already set up. Remove it on the Devices page first, so only one sensor reports the battery level.
wireless-battery.gaugeConflict: GP{{sda}} / GP{{scl}} can't be used for the fuel gauge, as {{conflicts}} is already in use. Add the gauge on the Devices page with free I2C pins instead.
wireless-battery.connectFirst: Connect your Pico to set this up.

wireless-bluetooth.title: Bluetooth Controller Setup
wireless-bluetooth.description: Turn on the Pico W's radio, make the active profile output over Bluetooth, then pair it with your PC or phone.
wireless-bluetooth.howText: Bluetooth output is part of a profile's assignments. It is added next to the profile's USB output, so the controller works over USB and Bluetooth at the same time.
pairSteps: Enable Bluetooth: Use the button on the right. The change applies to the connected Pico straight away.
Pair from the host: On your PC or phone, open the Bluetooth settings, add a new device and pick SantrollerBT.
Reconnecting: The host remembers the pairing and reconnects when the controller turns on. One host can be connected at a time, and the controller advertises again once it disconnects.
If pairing fails: Usually one side has forgotten the pairing (eg after the Pico was erased). Remove SantrollerBT from the host's Bluetooth settings and pair again.
wireless-bluetooth.syncNote: The Bluetooth device's optional pairing button pin (on the Devices page) only searches for Bluetooth controllers to connect to this Pico as inputs. Pairing it as a controller doesn't need one.
wireless-bluetooth.setupDesc: Adds the Bluetooth radio, and adds a Bluetooth output to each USB assignment list in the active profile ({{profile}}).
wireless-bluetooth.outputBadgeWiimote: Profile outputs over Bluetooth (Wii Remote mode)
wireless-bluetooth.outputMissing: Profile doesn't output over Bluetooth yet
wireless-bluetooth.inputsNote: The Inputs page shows the first output of each assignment list, so these lists still show as USB there. The Bluetooth output stays on as long as it is in the list.

wireless-power.title: Sleep & Power Saving
wireless-power.description: Turn Bluetooth off and put the Pico to sleep when the controller isn't being used.
optionsList: Bluetooth timeout: Turns the radio off after this long without a button press, while acting as a Bluetooth controller with no controllers connected to it. The next press turns it back on and reconnects.
Sleep: Puts the Pico into a deep sleep after this long without a button press, but only while it isn't plugged into USB. It needs a wake button, and pressing it restarts the controller.
LED timeout: Turns any LEDs off after this long, as they can be a big drain on the battery.
wireless-power.wakeTip: For the wake button, pick the pin of a button you have already wired (eg Start or Guide) that connects its pin to GND when pressed. Sleep still draws a little current, so fit a power switch if the controller will be stored for a long time.
wireless-power.powerMgmtTitle: Battery modules with a power button
wireless-power.powerMgmtText: If the controller runs from a charger / boost module with its own power button (eg a power bank style board) instead of a LiPo on VSYS, add a Battery Power Management device on the Devices page. It can press the module's power button to turn it off when idle, and pulse a load so the module doesn't switch itself off while you play.
wireless-power.btMissing: Set up Bluetooth in the previous step to set its timeout.
wireless-power.sleepActive: Sleep on: after {{seconds}} s on battery, wake with GP{{pin}}
wireless-power.sleepInactive: Sleep is off (it needs a timeout and a wake button pin)

wireless-test.title: Live Test & Save
wireless-test.description: Check the battery reading and the Bluetooth connection, then save the configuration to the Pico.
testSteps: Battery: The reading on the right updates about once a second. The GP29 monitor reads the USB voltage while plugged in and shows full, so check it on battery through the host's Bluetooth settings.
Bluetooth: Pair with your PC or phone. The status on the right shows when a host connects.
Save: Save to write the configuration to the Pico's flash, otherwise it is lost when the Pico restarts.
Go wireless: Unplug USB and run from the battery. The controller reconnects to the paired host by itself.
wireless-test.gaugeMissing: Fuel gauge not detected, check its I2C wiring
wireless-test.btNoOutput: The profile doesn't output over Bluetooth
wireless-test.btAdvertising: Waiting for a host to pair or connect
wireless-test.hostNote: A host connection also includes the configurator itself connecting over Bluetooth.
wireless-test.connectPrompt: Connect your Pico to see live status.

direct-pico-guitar.title: Direct-Wired Guitar (Raspberry Pi Pico)
direct-pico-guitar.subtitle: Interactive Wiring & Configuration Walkthrough
direct-pico-guitar.description: Step-by-step interactive build guide for rewiring any Guitar Hero or Rock Band guitar with mechanical or original switches to a Raspberry Pi Pico or Pico 2.

intro.title: 1. Getting Started & Standard Pinout
intro.description: Prepare your tools and microcontroller, and review the standard Santroller wiring plan.
intro.familyGh: Guitar Hero (Les Paul, WT, GH5, Xplorer)
intro.welcome: This guide covers converting or rewiring a Guitar Hero or Rock Band controller to a Raspberry Pi Pico or Pico 2.
intro.directRewireCaption: A direct-wired mechanical switch guitar with a Raspberry Pi Pico
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2: Any standard RP2040 or RP2350 board.
Soldering iron & solder: 60/40 or lead-free.
Wire (26-30 AWG): Stranded or solid core wire.
Multimeter: Used in continuity mode (the mode that beeps when probes touch) to trace common grounds and signals.
Wire strippers & cutters: For prepping hookup wires.
rules: Find Common Ground: Use a multimeter in continuity mode to identify shared ground traces or wires.
Trace Signal Wires: Trace signal wires for each switch or potentiometer.
Solder & Verify: Solder to your chosen GP pin, then test.
intro.pinoutDesc: Use the default Santroller pin layout or choose your own GPIO pins.

frets.title: 2. Fret Buttons & Slider
frets.description: Connect the 5 fret buttons (Green, Red, Yellow, Blue, Orange) and optional touch slider bar, then verify each input in real time.
frets.intro: The frets are simple mechanical or membrane switches. Each colour has its own signal wire, and the other side of every switch goes to ground. That makes 6 wires to the Pico: 5 fret signals and 1 ground.
frets.introRb: Wire every fret straight to its own Pico pin. Rock Band necks have two rows of frets, each with its own ground, so this takes 12 wires: 5 upper fret signals + 1 upper ground, and 5 solo fret signals + 1 solo ground. Both grounds go to Pico GND. On a stock neck the solo frets share the 7-wire harness, so you need to run dedicated wires from the lower (solo) fret PCB to the body.
frets.pcbCaption: Example neck PCB (Xplorer): each fret has its own coloured signal trace, while the black ground traces are split across several connector pins
frets.stepGround: Identify Ground: If the neck cable or PCB is not labelled, inspect the neck PCB traces. Ground is not always one trace looping past every switch; as on the Xplorer neck above, it can be split into several traces (black) that each reach their own connector pin.
frets.stepMultimeter: Confirm with Multimeter: In continuity mode, touch one probe to a ground pin and the other to a fret wire. Pressing that fret should beep. Check each fret, as different frets may use different ground pins.
frets.stepSolderGround: Solder Ground: Connect every ground pin from the neck to a GND pin on the Raspberry Pi Pico (e.g., Pin 3 or Pin 8). They can share one GND pin.
frets.stepSolderSignals: Solder Fret Signals: Connect each coloured fret signal wire to an unused digital GPIO pin. Our recommended standard uses:
frets.pullUpText: Santroller automatically configures internal pull-up resistors on the Pico for all digital buttons, so you do not need any external resistors. When you press a fret, it shorts the GP pin to Ground.
frets.benchHint: Assign pins manually or click Probe and press the fret button on your guitar to auto-detect its wiring:
frets.gh5Intro: Guitar Hero 5 necks feature a 4-wire digital bus that communicates over I2C. This carries the 5 fret buttons AND the capacitive touch slider bar over just two data pins plus power with zero neck modifications.
frets.gh5PinGnd: GND → Pico Pin 38 (or any GND pin)
frets.gh5VoltageWarning: Always use 3.3V (Pin 36). Never connect the neck to 5V (VBUS); doing so will permanently damage the neck controller IC.
frets.gh5DriverCardDesc: Enable Santroller's built-in GH5 neck driver to automatically configure I2C on GP18/GP19 and map both the frets and the touch slider bar.
frets.gh5DriverActive: I2C Driver Active (GP18 SDA / GP19 SCL)
frets.rbSoloIntro: Stock Rock Band guitars with solo frets use a 7-wire harness: 5 fret signal lines, 1 upper fret common, and 1 solo fret common. Santroller scans this directly as a 5x2 matrix across 5 fret signal columns (GP2-GP6) and 2 row outputs (GP14 Upper, GP15 Solo), reading all 10 frets with no trace cutting required. The neck has no diodes, so holding an upper and a solo fret of the same colour at the same time connects GP14 to GP15 through the two switches while they are scanned: that colour reads unreliably and the two row outputs briefly drive against each other. Avoid holding both frets of one colour, or use the split neck method if you need them together.
frets.rbSoloMatrixNoGnd: Do not connect the neck common wires to Pico GND. The Pico drives them dynamically as matrix row outputs.
frets.rbSoloDriverDesc: Enable Santroller's built-in Matrix driver to configure GP2-GP6 as column inputs and GP14/GP15 as row outputs, mapping all 10 frets automatically.
frets.rbSoloDriverActive: Matrix Driver Active (GP2-GP6 In / GP14-GP15 Out)
frets.rbShiftedIntro: Some 7-pin Rock Band necks share a common Ground with a dedicated Solo switch line. When a solo fret is pressed, it shorts both that fret's signal and the Solo line to Ground. Santroller models this via Shifted Inputs: normal frets trigger when the fret is pressed without Solo, while solo frets trigger when both are pressed.
frets.rbShiftedDriverDesc: Configure all 10 frets automatically using Shifted inputs on GP2-GP6 with GP12 as the Solo modifier.
frets.mpr121Intro: Guitar Hero World Tour guitars used a single-wire analog slider bar with high latency and limited chord detection. Bypassing the stock chip with an MPR121 capacitive touch breakout over I2C provides ultra-low latency multi-touch tracking.
frets.mpr121StepTraces: Cut traces leading away from chip U2 (or desolder U2 entirely) on the slider PCB as shown in the diagram.
frets.mpr121TracesCaption: Trace cuts around U2 on the World Tour slider PCB
frets.mpr121StepVias: Solder wires from each via (channels 0 through 4) on the slider PCB to channels 0-4 on the MPR121 breakout.
frets.mpr121ViasCaption: Slider via locations to solder to MPR121 channels 0-4
frets.mpr121I2cTitle: 3. MPR121 to Raspberry Pi Pico Connections
frets.mpr121StepFrets: The MPR121 only handles the slider. Wire the 5 fret buttons and their ground directly to the Pico (GP2-GP6), exactly as in Direct GPIO mode, and test them in the panel on the right.
frets.mpr121StepI2c: Connect the MPR121 to the Pico over I2C: 3.3V (Pin 36), GND (Pin 38), SDA (GP18 / Pin 24), and SCL (GP19 / Pin 25).
frets.mpr121DriverDesc: Add an MPR121 on I2C (GP18 SDA / GP19 SCL) and map its channels 0-4 to the five slider zones.

strum.title: 3. Strum Bar Switches
strum.description: Connect Strum Up and Strum Down switches, cut board traces if reusing original PCBs, and test switch actuation.
strum.intro: The strum bar is operated by two switches: Strum Up and Strum Down. Like the frets, these two switches share a common ground wire.
strum.strumPcbCaption: Strum switches on an original main PCB
strum.directIntro: When using replacement mechanical switches (like Kailh Box switches) or a 3D-printed strum bracket, the switches are completely isolated from stock circuitry.
strum.directStepGround: Common Ground: Connect one pin of each switch together and wire to any GND pin on the Pico.
strum.directStepUp: Strum Up: Connect the signal contact to GP7 (Pin 10).
strum.directStepDown: Strum Down: Connect the signal contact to GP8 (Pin 11).
strum.cutTraceDesc1: If your strum switches are soldered directly to an original console PCB (such as Wii, Xbox 360, or PS3), they remain connected to the original console microcontroller and capacitors. This causes phantom or stuck inputs unless traces are cut.
strum.cutTraceDesc2: Use a craft knife or razor to score and sever the copper traces leading away from the switch pins. Use your multimeter in continuity mode to confirm each switch contact is isolated from the rest of the board.
strum.cutTraceCaption: Cutting copper traces around strum switch contacts
strum.benchHint: Assign pins manually or flick the strum bar to auto-detect the switch:
strum.debounceDesc: Mechanical strum switches can bounce on release, causing unwanted double strums. You can fine-tune Strum Debounce in Profile Poll Settings if you notice accidental over-strums.

whammy.title: 4. Whammy Bar Potentiometer
whammy.description: Wire the 10k potentiometer to 3.3V, Ground, and ADC0 (GP26), then test live analog movement.
whammy.intro: The whammy bar connects to an analog potentiometer (typically 10kΩ). Unlike digital buttons, which are either on or off, the whammy measures variable depth and must connect to one of the Pico's dedicated Analog ADC pins.
whammy.potCenter: Centre Pin (Signal / Wiper): Solder to GP26 (ADC0 / Pin 31) on your Pico.
whammy.potOuter1: Outer Pin 1: Solder to 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36) on your Pico.
whammy.potOuter2: Outer Pin 2: Solder to GND (Pin 38) on your Pico.
whammy.invertNote: (Note: If the whammy value decreases when pressed instead of increasing, you can either swap the two outer wires or toggle "Invert" in calibration.)
whammy.warning2WireDesc: Some stock guitars have a potentiometer PCB where two pins are bridged, leaving only 2 wires exposed. You must desolder the bridged connection and solder 3 distinct wires directly to the 3 potentiometer pins.
whammy.warning2WireCaption: Desoldering bridged pins to wire 3 full lines (3V3, Signal, GND)
whammy.pickupIntro: Rock Band Stratocaster and Precision Bass guitars include a 5-way pickup selector switch for guitar effects. Like the whammy, it connects to an analog ADC pin (GP27 / ADC1).
whammy.pickupCenter: Signal / Wiper Pin: Connect to GP27 (ADC1 / Pin 32).
whammy.pickup2WireDesc: On the Rock Band Precision Bass, the pickup potentiometer PCB bridges two pins. Desolder the small attached PCB and run 3 distinct wires directly from the potentiometer pins to 3.3V, GP27, and GND.
whammy.benchHint: Verify analog ADC input. Move the whammy bar to watch the live progress bar respond:
whammy.verificationDesc: When wired correctly, releasing the whammy should show a steady low or high value, and pressing the whammy bar will smoothly increase or decrease the reading.

tilt.title: 5. Star Power Tilt Sensor
tilt.description: Connect a ball tilt switch to GP11 or an I2C accelerometer to trigger Star Power / Overdrive.
tilt.intro: Tilt sensors activate Star Power / Overdrive when you tilt the guitar neck upward. Santroller supports digital ball tilt switches and I2C accelerometers.
tilt.digitalIntro: A ball tilt switch (such as the SW-520D) opens or closes when tilted at roughly 45°.
tilt.seriesTipTitle: Tip: Wire two switches in series
tilt.seriesTipDesc: To prevent false triggers from hard strumming, wire two tilt switches in series. Both switches must close simultaneously to trigger Star Power.
tilt.digitalPinGnd: Connect one pin of the tilt sensor to any GND on the Pico.
tilt.digitalPinGp: Connect the other pin to GP11 (Pin 15).
tilt.digitalMount: Mount the sensor inside the guitar body angled slightly upward towards the neck.
tilt.i2cIntro: Accelerometers measure gravitational acceleration along 3 axes for tilt detection.
tilt.i2cShared: A GH5 neck or MPR121 slider can share these SDA / SCL pins with the accelerometer; connect them in parallel.
tilt.accelDriverDesc: Add an accelerometer (ADXL345, LIS3DH or MPU-6050) on I2C (GP18 SDA / GP19 SCL) and drive tilt from its X axis.
tilt.accelBenchHint: Raw accelerometer reading (tilt the neck up and down):
tilt.accelAxisDesc: Tilt is read from the X axis, with level as no tilt and the X axis pointing straight up as full tilt. If the reading barely moves when you lift the neck, or moves the wrong way, change the axis or swap the minimum and maximum on the Tilt input in the Inputs page.
tilt.benchHint: Tilt the guitar body upward to test activation:
tilt.invertDesc: If your tilt sensor triggers when resting and turns off when lifted, toggle "Invert" in the input settings.

nav.title: 6. Start, Select & Menu Navigation
nav.description: Wire the Start and Select buttons to GP9 and GP10, and optionally configure the Home combo.
nav.intro: Start (Pause / Plus) and Select (Star Power / Minus) buttons let you navigate menus and pause songs.
nav.navGround: Find Common Ground: Follow the traces between the Start and Select contacts or use continuity mode on your multimeter. Connect the common ground to any GND pin on the Pico.
nav.startSignal: Start Button Signal: Connect the Start signal wire to GP9 (Pin 12).
nav.selectSignal: Select Button Signal: Connect the Select signal wire to GP10 (Pin 14).
nav.comboDesc: You can configure a shortcut in Santroller to map Start + Select to the Guide / Home button if your guitar lacks a dedicated guide button.
nav.benchHint: Assign pins or click Probe and press Start or Select to test:

review.title: 7. Complete & Final Verification
review.description: Verify all guitar inputs and save your configuration to the Pico.
review.finalVerificationDesc: Use the diagnostic panel on the right to test every switch, strum, and the whammy bar. Press chord combinations and flick the strum bar up and down rapidly to ensure clean actuation.
review.saveDesc: When all inputs test correctly, click Save Configuration to Pico Flash to write your settings to flash memory.
review.saveErrorFallback: Failed to save configuration to controller
review.savedSuccessDesc: Configuration saved to Pico flash memory.

wii-adapter.title: Wii Controller & Guitar to USB Adapter
wii-adapter.subtitle: Plug-and-Play I2C Adapter for Wii Guitars
wii-adapter.description: Build an adapter using a Raspberry Pi Pico to use any Wii Guitar Hero or Rock Band guitar on PC or console with zero soldering to the guitar itself.

wii-intro.title: 1. Supplies & Overview
wii-intro.description: Learn the 4-wire I2C pinout needed to adapt any Wii controller to USB.
wii-intro.intro: The Wii Guitar Adapter lets you plug any original Nintendo Wii guitar (Les Paul, World Tour, GH5) or Classic Controller into a Raspberry Pi Pico and use it on PC or consoles with ultra-low latency.
wii-intro.adapterCaption: A completed Wii controller adapter powered by a Pi Pico
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Wii Extension Breakout Board or cut extension cable
Soldering Iron & 4 wires
wii-intro.noDisassemblyText: Building an external adapter requires zero modifications to your guitar. The guitar's original Wii connector plugs directly into the adapter.
wii-intro.quickStartDesc: Wii controllers communicate over I2C. Connect 4 wires between the Wii connector and Pico:

wii-wiring.title: 2. Wii Connector Pinout & Wiring
wii-wiring.description: Wire 3.3V, Ground, SDA, and SCL, and add the Wii guitar to your profile.
wii-wiring.intro: Connect the 4 wires from your Wii female connector or breakout board to the Raspberry Pi Pico.
wii-wiring.socketCaption: Extension socket pin numbers (the end your controller plugs into)
wii-wiring.plugCaption: Controller plug pinout, looking into the plug. A4 / A5 are Arduino labels: on the Pico, SDA goes to GP18 and SCL to GP19.

drum-kit.title: Drum Kit & E-Drums (Piezo & Multiplexer)
drum-kit.subtitle: Velocity-Sensitive Drum Kit with Multiplexers
drum-kit.description: Build a custom velocity-sensitive electronic drum kit or rewire an existing Rock Band or Guitar Hero kit to a Raspberry Pi Pico.

drum-intro.title: 1. Supplies & Drum Architecture
drum-intro.description: Understanding piezo velocity sensors, protection diodes, and multiplexer expansion.
drum-intro.intro: Build a custom drum kit or convert existing Guitar Hero / Rock Band drum pads using a Raspberry Pi Pico. Each pad uses a piezo, which gives a voltage pulse that grows with how hard you hit it. The Pico only has three ADC pins (GP26 - GP28), so every piezo goes through one analog multiplexer, which lets a single ADC pin read all of the pads with velocity, kick pedal included.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Piezoelectric Sensors (1 per drum pad / cymbal / kick)
1MΩ Resistors (1 per piezo to pull signal to ground)
3.3V Zener Diodes (1 per piezo, to protect the multiplexer and Pico from high voltage spikes)
Analog Multiplexer: a 74HC4051 / CD4051 (8 channels) or 74HC4067 / CD4067 (16 channels)
drum-intro.mux4051Caption: 4051 8-channel analog multiplexer pinout (Z is the common pin)
drum-intro.layoutDesc: Wire each pad's piezo to the multiplexer channel below. The guide's setup button maps the pads to these channels.
drum-intro.otherKitsTitle: Band Hero or World Tour kit?
drum-intro.otherKitsText: These kits can be converted without hardwiring piezos. For a Band Hero / Guitar Hero 5 era kit, use the Band Hero Drum Kit guide instead. For a Guitar Hero World Tour kit, use the World Tour Drum Kit guide. An e-drum kit with a 5-pin MIDI OUT port doesn't need hardwired piezos either: use the MIDI In (5-pin DIN) guide to connect its MIDI OUT to the Pico.

drum-wiring.title: 2. Piezo & Multiplexer Wiring
drum-wiring.description: Connect each piezo with a 1MΩ resistor and 3.3V zener diode to a multiplexer channel, then wire the multiplexer to the Pico.
drum-wiring.intro: Piezos generate an analog voltage pulse proportional to how hard you hit the drum pad. Each piezo gets its own resistor and zener diode, then connects to one multiplexer channel.
drum-wiring.polarityWarningText: Piezo discs are directional. Connect the outer brass ring (black wire) to Ground and the inner ceramic disc (red wire) to the multiplexer channel. If hits register weakly, swap the wires.
wiringSteps: Black Wire to Ground: Connect the outer brass ring (black wire) to a common GND.
Red Wire to the Multiplexer: Connect the inner ceramic disc (red wire) to the pad's multiplexer channel from the layout table.
1MΩ Resistor: Connect a 1MΩ resistor between the signal line and ground to pull the line low when not hit.
3.3V Zener Diode: Connect a 3.3V zener diode between signal and ground (cathode to signal, anode to ground) to clamp spikes over 3.3V.
muxSteps: Common: Connect the multiplexer's common pin (Z on a 4051, COMMON / SIG on a 4067) to GP{{com}} (Pin {{comPhysical}}, ADC0).
Select Pins: Connect S0 to GP{{s0}} (Pin {{s0Physical}}), S1 to GP{{s1}} (Pin {{s1Physical}}), and S2 to GP{{s2}} (Pin {{s2Physical}}). A 4067 also needs S3 on GP{{s3}} (Pin {{s3Physical}}).
Power: Connect VCC to 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36) and GND to a Pico GND pin.
Enable & VEE: Connect the enable pin (E with a bar over it, sometimes INH) to GND so the chip is always on. A 4051 also has a VEE pin: connect it to GND too.
Channels: Channel 0 is Y0 on a 4051, and I0 on a 4067. Leave unused channels unconnected, or tie them to GND.
drum-wiring.slowText: CD40xx multiplexers switch channels more slowly than 74HC parts at 3.3V. Picking a CD part in the setup sets the multiplexer's Slow option, so the firmware waits for the reading to settle after switching channels (at the cost of slower polling). It can also be changed later on the Devices page.
drum-wiring.setupDesc: Pick your kit type and multiplexer chip. This adds the multiplexer (common on GP26, select pins on GP2 - GP4, plus GP5 for a 4067), switches the profile to the chosen drum kit, and maps each pad to its channel with a starting strike threshold. Pads that already have a mapping are moved to the multiplexer.
drum-wiring.setupProgress: {{mapped}} of {{total}} pads mapped to the multiplexer
drum-wiring.hitMonitorDesc: Tap the pads to verify velocity response. Each bar shows the raw reading of that pad's input, held briefly after a hit.

drum-test.title: 3. Live Test & Save
drum-test.description: Perform strike tests across all pads, then save to Pico flash.
drum-test.calibratedText: The setup mapped each pad with a starting strike threshold. Strike every pad and check its bar on the right, then save the configuration to the Pico.
drum-test.tipsText: Each pad's deadzone on the Inputs page is its strike threshold (a Rock Band kick uses its trigger value instead). If a pad triggers on its own, or hitting one drum triggers an adjacent one (cross-talk), raise that pad's deadzone or debounce there.
